claim: New species arise as the genomes of populations diverge.
source: New species arise as the genomes of populations diverge.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that represents established scientific consensus about speciation.

claim: The developmental 'alarm clock' of speciation sounds off when sufficient divergence in genetic control of development leads hybrid individuals to infertility or inviability.
source: The developmental 'alarm clock' of speciation sounds off when sufficient divergence in genetic control of development leads hybrid individuals to infertility or inviability, the world awoken to the dawn of new species with intrinsic post-zygotic reproductive isolation.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework presented by the authors to describe the relationship between developmental divergence and reproductive isolation.

claim: Some developmental stages will be more prone to hybrid dysfunction due to how molecular evolution interacts with the ontogenetic timing of gene expression.
source: Some developmental stages will be more prone to hybrid dysfunction due to how molecular evolution interacts with the ontogenetic timing of gene expression.
evidence: This is a central hypothesis of the manuscript that is explored throughout the text.

claim: Darwin recognized the dilemma that natural selection will oppose changes that confer a net fitness cost.
source: Darwin recognized this dilemma (Darwin 1859), in that natural selection will oppose changes that confer a net fitness cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Darwin's work.

claim: Evolution can circumvent the problem of fitness costs through interactions between multiple genetic factors, as made explicit in the genetic mechanism of Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibility (DMI) for post-zygotic disruption in hybrids.
source: But evolution can circumvent this problem through interactions between multiple genetic factors, as intuited by W. Bateson, T. Dobzhansky and H.J. Muller and made explicit in the genetic mechanism of Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibility (DMI) for post-zygotic disruption in hybrids (Box 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to established theory and historical scientific work.

claim: When evolution substitutes an allele at one locus, it makes no guarantee that this new derived genetic background will be compatible with allele substitutions occurring in other populations at other loci.
source: Put simply: when evolution substitutes an allele at one locus, it makes no guarantee that this new derived genetic background will be compatible with allele substitutions occurring in other populations at other loci.
evidence: This is an explanation of the Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibility mechanism based on established theory.

claim: Incompatible combinations of alleles in hybrid individuals at two or more loci can be thought of as negative epistasis or as a kind of non-linear genetic perturbation.
source: Incompatible combinations of alleles in hybrid individuals at two or more loci can be thought of as negative epistasis or as a kind of non-linear genetic perturbation.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of genetic incompatibilities based on established genetic principles.

claim: The genetics of speciation sound similar to notions of cryptic genetic variation and developmental system drift in the literature on the evolution of development.
source: Put this way, the genetics of speciation sound eerily similar to notions of cryptic genetic variation (Wade et al., 1997; Ledón-Rettig et al., 2014; Paaby and Rockman, 2014) and developmental system drift in the literature on the evolution of development (True and Haag, 2001; Pavlicev and Wagner, 2012; Tulchinsky et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim connects concepts from different fields and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The regulatory pathways that govern development are an important component of how and whether divergence will lead to genetic incompatibility and speciation.
source: The regulatory pathways that govern development are an important component of how and whether divergence will lead to genetic incompatibility and speciation (Porter and Johnson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Conservation of phenotype does not imply conservation of genetic controls.
source: The converse, however, is not true: conservation of phenotype does not imply conservation of genetic controls.
evidence: This is a key principle in evolutionary developmental biology supported by the subsequent example.

claim: Stabilizing selection on expression levels leads to similar expression levels between species, despite evidence of widespread compensatory effects of molecular evolution to both cis- and trans-acting regulators of gene expression.
source: For example, stabilizing selection on expression levels leads to similar expression levels between species, despite evidence of widespread compensatory effects of molecular evolution to both cis- and trans-acting regulators of gene expression (Mack and Nachman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: Adaptive evolution at the molecular level can contribute to developmental system drift for a given trait, particularly if the genetic changes affect fitness through pleiotropic effects with phenotypic consequences for only a subset of traits or from subsequent compensatory evolution.
source: Adaptive evolution at the molecular level also can contribute to DSD for a given trait, particularly if the genetic changes affect fitness through pleiotropic effects with phenotypic consequences for only a subset of traits or from subsequent compensatory evolution (Box 1C).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about mechanisms of developmental system drift.

claim: Each mutational substitution that distinguishes species in protein coding sequence or gene regulatory control has some probability of contributing to the formation of a DMI in hybrid individuals.
source: Each mutational substitution that distinguishes species in protein coding sequence or gene regulatory control thus has some probability of contributing to the formation of a DMI in hybrid individuals.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the theory of Dobzhansky-Muller incompatibilities.

claim: The more substitutions, the more chances for incompatibilities to create hybrid dysfunction at some point in development.
source: The more substitutions, the more chances for incompatibilities to create hybrid dysfunction at some point in development (Orr, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work by Orr.

claim: Inter-species hybrids can reveal genetic divergence in the control of even those developmental programs that yield seemingly equivalent phenotypic outputs.
source: In this way, inter-species hybrids can reveal genetic divergence in the control of even those developmental programs that yield seemingly equivalent phenotypic outputs.
evidence: This is an inference about what hybrids can reveal about cryptic genetic divergence.

claim: Hybrids can reveal the incidence and role of different kinds of changes, such as cis- vs trans-acting regulators of gene expression.
source: Hybrids can also reveal the incidence and role of different kinds of changes, such as cis- vs trans-acting regulators of gene expression (Box 2; Wittkopp et al., 2004; Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The extent of pleiotropic effects induced by mutation to a gene is a major determinant of the likelihood of evolutionary change to that gene.
source: The extent of pleiotropic effects induced by mutation to a gene is a major determinant of the likelihood of evolutionary change to that gene (Carroll, 2005; Stern and Orgogozo, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Most traits experience stabilizing selection on short timescales, and so the effects of mutation on most traits will be detrimental and offset any fitness benefit conferred to a particular trait by a mutation.
source: This logic follows from the idea that most traits experience stabilizing selection on short timescales, and so the effects of mutation on most traits will be detrimental and offset any fitness benefit conferred to a particular trait by a mutation.
evidence: This is a principle from evolutionary theory about the nature of selection on traits.

claim: On longer timescales, conserved traits are thought to track a moving but bounded fitness landscape, which can facilitate compensatory evolution among the collection of interacting genes of the genetic network to result in sequence divergence and reproductive isolation between populations.
source: On longer timescales, conserved traits are thought to track a moving but bounded fitness landscape (Estes and Arnold, 2007), which can facilitate compensatory evolution among the collection of interacting genes of the genetic network to result in sequence divergence and reproductive isolation between populations (Haag and Molla, 2005; Tulchinsky et al., 2014a; Tulchinsky et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: More rapid evolution should occur in genes with fewer pleiotropic roles or for classes of changes that perturb fewer of a gene's roles.
source: Consequently, we might expect that more rapid evolution should occur in genes with fewer pleiotropic roles or for classes of changes that perturb fewer of a gene's roles.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the logic of pleiotropy and selection.

claim: The position of a gene within gene regulatory networks defines the pleiotropic roles it plays in development.
source: The position of a gene within gene regulatory networks defines the pleiotropic roles it plays in development.
evidence: This is a principle about how network position relates to pleiotropy.

claim: Genes in more central and highly connected network positions can influence a greater fraction of the genome, and so changes to those genes have the potential to induce greater pleiotropic effects.
source: Genes in more central and highly connected network positions can influence a greater fraction of the genome, and so changes to those genes have the potential to induce greater pleiotropic effects (Promislow, 2004; Hahn and Kern, 2005; He and Zhang, 2006; Kahali et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The precise relationship between centrality and pleiotropy remains complex.
source: However, the precise relationship between centrality and pleiotropy remains complex (Siegal et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim acknowledges complexity and is supported by citation.

claim: Despite the idea that network 'kernels' may perdure through evolution, the molecular interactions among kernel components may nevertheless coevolve in ways that could generate DMIs.
source: And, despite the idea that network 'kernels' may perdure through evolution (Erwin and Davidson, 2009), the molecular interactions among kernel components may nevertheless coevolve in ways that could generate DMIs (Haag, 2007; Tulchinsky et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Genes that are expressed at high levels are more likely to have a large number of interaction partners and therefore to occupy central network positions.
source: Genes that are expressed at high levels also are more likely to have a large number of interaction partners and therefore to occupy central network positions (Bloom and Adami, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Coding sequence changes can affect protein activity everywhere they get expressed, and so ought to have greater potential for pleiotropic effects than regulatory changes.
source: Coding sequence changes can affect protein activity everywhere they get expressed, and so ought to have greater potential for pleiotropic effects than regulatory changes (Wray et al., 2003; Carroll, 2005; Stern and Orgogozo, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a key principle in evolutionary developmental biology.

claim: Alterations of cis-regulatory elements generally influence only a subset of a gene's expression, and so will exert the fewest pleiotropic effects relative to coding sequence and trans-regulatory changes.
source: Alterations of cis-regulatory elements, in contrast, generally influence only a subset of a gene's expression, and so will exert the fewest pleiotropic effects relative to coding sequence and trans-regulatory changes.
evidence: This is a principle about the relative pleiotropic effects of different types of mutations.

claim: Trans-regulatory evolution and coding sequence divergence ought generally to be slower for genes with high centrality and connectivity in genetic networks.
source: Consequently, trans-regulatory evolution and coding sequence divergence ought generally to be slower for genes with high centrality and connectivity in genetic networks.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the logic of pleiotropy and network position.

claim: Trans-acting regulation tends to show greater condition-dependence than does cis-regulation.
source: Because trans-acting regulation tends to show greater condition-dependence than does cis-regulation (Smith and Kruglyak, 2008; Tirosh et al., 2009), however, pleiotropy-based predictions for their evolution may be tempered by the fact that varying conditions experienced by organisms could limit the net negative pleiotropic effects of trans-regulatory changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Trans-regulatory evolution may often be coupled to subsequent cis-regulatory compensatory evolution that ameliorates negative pleiotropic effects of a population having fixed a beneficial trans-regulatory change.
source: Moreover, trans-regulatory evolution may often be coupled to subsequent cis-regulatory compensatory evolution that ameliorates negative pleiotropic effects of a population having fixed a beneficial trans-regulatory change.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about compensatory evolution patterns.

claim: Compensatory evolution involving both cis- and trans-acting regulatory evolution may be an especially important contributor to DMI formation.
source: Such compensatory evolution involving both cis- and trans-acting regulatory evolution may be an especially important contributor to DMI formation (Landry et al., 2005; Ortíz-Barrientos et al., 2006; Takahasi et al., 2011; Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical and theoretical work.

claim: Experiments show that trans-acting regulatory factors contribute disproportionately to segregating genetic variation for gene expression levels within species, whereas cis-acting regulatory differences disproportionately underlie fixed genetic differences in expression between species.
source: Experiments show that trans-acting regulatory factors contribute disproportionately to segregating genetic variation for gene expression levels within species, whereas cis-acting regulatory differences disproportionately underlie fixed genetic differences in expression between species (Wittkopp and Kalay, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of experimental evidence.

claim: To the extent that regulatory evolution is responsible for creating DMIs, we ought to expect polymorphic DMIs to often be controlled by trans-acting factors.
source: The loci controlling DMIs also can be polymorphic or fixed (Cutter, 2012), and so to the extent that regulatory evolution is responsible for creating DMIs, we ought to expect polymorphic DMIs to often be controlled by trans-acting factors.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the patterns of cis vs trans regulatory variation.

claim: Trans-regulatory mutations tend to arise more readily due to larger mutational target size in the genome, and to be more recessive, than cis-acting mutations.
source: Because trans-regulatory mutations tend to arise more readily due to larger mutational target size in the genome, and to be more recessive, than cis-acting mutations (Landry et al., 2007; Gruber et al., 2012), they are expected to be a common and persistent kind of polymorphism within populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Modularity of genetic networks reduces the scope for genes to have highly pleiotropic roles.
source: Modularity of genetic networks reduces the scope for genes to have highly pleiotropic roles (Wagner and Altenberg, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Greater modularity limits the pleiotropic effects of changes to gene expression or function for any given gene by constraining the neighborhood of partner interactions.
source: By constraining the neighborhood of partner interactions, greater modularity limits the pleiotropic effects of changes to gene expression or function for any given gene.
evidence: This is an explanation of how modularity affects pleiotropy.

claim: Modularity of genetic network structure will increase over ontogeny as cells differentiate and tissues establish autonomous regulatory programs.
source: Modularity of genetic network structure will increase over ontogeny as cells differentiate and tissues establish autonomous regulatory programs (Packer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: Some transient phases of development are thought to reverse the trend of increasing modularity, as when tissues integrate during gastrulation or reorganize during metamorphosis.
source: Some transient phases of development are thought to reverse this trend, however, as when tissues integrate during gastrulation or reorganize during metamorphosis (Chin-Sang and Chisholm, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: If pleiotropy at the scale of the whole organism constrains evolution of individual genes, then we might expect faster molecular evolution for genes that experience highly modular genetic network structures due to spatially- or temporally restricted expression.
source: Consequently, if pleiotropy at the scale of the whole organism constrains evolution of individual genes, then we might expect faster molecular evolution for genes that experience highly modular genetic network structures due to spatially- or temporally restricted expression.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the relationship between modularity and pleiotropy.

claim: Genes with greater breadth of expression across tissues, and genes with greater temporal persistence of expression, will experience more scope to contribute to different genetic networks and their phenotypic outputs.
source: Genes with greater breadth of expression across tissues, and genes with greater temporal persistence of expression, will experience more scope to contribute to different genetic networks and their phenotypic outputs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how expression patterns relate to network participation.

claim: Genes most likely to produce pleiotropic effects when genetically perturbed are those expressed at high levels across many tissues throughout a long span of developmental time (high expression breadth and low temporal expression bias).
source: Consequently, genes most likely to produce pleiotropic effects when genetically perturbed are those expressed at high levels across many tissues throughout a long span of developmental time (high expression breadth and low temporal expression bias; Larracuente et al., 2008; Coronado-Zamora et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: A genetically 'robust' phenotype is insensitive to genetic perturbations, which permits an organism to produce the same phenotype and to maintain fitness despite mutational disruption to a gene or genetic network that contributes to the trait's developmental program.
source: A genetically 'robust' phenotype is insensitive to genetic perturbations, which permits an organism to produce the same phenotype and to maintain fitness despite mutational disruption to a gene or genetic network that contributes to the trait's developmental program (Félix and Wagner, 2008).
evidence: This is a definition of genetic robustness supported by citation.

claim: A greater fraction of mutations to genes in more robust networks have effectively neutral effects.
source: That is, a greater fraction of mutations to genes in more robust networks have effectively neutral effects (Ohta, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: A gene network's robustness ought to influence the mutations that can accumulate, which in turn affects rates of molecular evolutionary divergence and the manifestation of genetic incompatibilities in hybrids.
source: A gene network's robustness therefore ought to influence the mutations that can accumulate, which in turn affects rates of molecular evolutionary divergence and the manifestation of genetic incompatibilities in hybrids.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of robustness for evolution.

claim: Differences across gene networks in genetic robustness could arise from differential selection on robustness itself (adaptive robustness or canalization) or could simply arise as a byproduct of differences in their epistatic genetic architectures.
source: Differences across gene networks in genetic robustness could arise from differential selection on robustness itself (adaptive robustness or canalization) or could simply arise as a byproduct of differences in their epistatic genetic architectures (Hermisson and Wagner, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Genes and genetic networks that are more robust to genetic perturbation can be thought of as larger phenotypic capacitors, letting more cryptic genetic divergence in developmental controls accumulate to be revealed upon the formation of inter-species hybrids.
source: Genes and genetic networks that are more robust to genetic perturbation can be thought of as larger phenotypic capacitors (Paaby and Testa, 2018), letting more cryptic genetic divergence in developmental controls accumulate to be revealed upon the formation of inter-species hybrids.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a conceptual framework.

claim: Traits with greater genetic robustness ought to accumulate more cryptic genetic variation within a species that can then contribute to greater developmental system drift between species as substitutions accrue.
source: As a consequence, traits with greater genetic robustness ought to accumulate more cryptic genetic variation within a species that can then can contribute to greater developmental system drift between species as substitutions accrue (Félix and Wagner, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents a prediction about robustness and DSD.

claim: More robust networks are more likely to contain more cryptic genetic variation.
source: More robust networks are more likely to contain more cryptic genetic variation, but the presence of cryptic genetic variation alone is insufficient to conclude whether or not selection directly favored greater robustness, and characterizing the robustness of genetic networks empirically can be difficult.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between robustness and cryptic variation, with caveats.

claim: The selective regime that shapes the fitness landscape will influence the speed at which developmental system drift can evolve for any given trait.
source: The selective regime that shapes the fitness landscape will influence the speed at which developmental system drift can evolve for any given trait (Tulchinsky et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: DSD is especially likely to result from directional selection on traits, perhaps facilitated by a role for cryptic genetic variation in adaptation to environmental shifts, and from selection that drives molecular co-evolution among genetic elements.
source: DSD is especially likely to result from directional selection on traits, perhaps facilitated by a role for cryptic genetic variation in adaptation to environmental shifts (Félix and Wagner, 2008), and from selection that drives molecular co-evolution among genetic elements (Tulchinsky et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Phenotypes with a larger underlying genetic network are expected to be more robust to perturbation.
source: Phenotypes with a larger underlying genetic network are expected to be more robust to perturbation (Fragata et al., 2019), implying that they should more readily tolerate the accumulation of genetic changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Genes holding more central positions in genetic networks appear to be associated with greater robustness upon perturbation, although this effect may depend more on expression level than connectivity per se.
source: Genes holding more central positions in genetic networks also appear to be associated with greater robustness upon perturbation (Proulx et al., 2007), although this effect may depend more on expression level than connectivity per se (Siegal et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Changes to any given gene in a network that is shared with other networks, and that confers a beneficial effect to that other network, are less likely to manifest negative pleiotropic effects for those genetic networks that are larger.
source: This means that changes to any given gene in a network that is shared with other networks, and that confers a beneficial effect to that other network, are less likely to manifest negative pleiotropic effects for those genetic networks that are larger (Pavlicev and Wagner, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Cryptic variation and DSD may be disproportionately prevalent in developmental programs comprised of larger genetic networks.
source: Consequently, cryptic variation and DSD may be disproportionately prevalent in developmental programs comprised of larger genetic networks.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the relationship between network size and robustness.

claim: Genetic networks with low modularity are most robust to genetic perturbation.
source: Genetic networks with low modularity, by definition, have all constituent genes interacting, and networks with low modularity indeed are most robust to genetic perturbation (Tran and Kwon, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: Genetic networks with switch-like behavior may be more capable of accumulating cryptic variation, as appears to occur disproportionately among genes with early zygotic expression in sea urchin embryogenesis.
source: For example, genetic networks with switch-like behavior may be more capable of accumulating cryptic variation, as appears to occur disproportionately among genes with early zygotic expression in sea urchin embryogenesis (Garfield et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: Ontogenetic stages that have an especially high incidence of mutationally-robust phenotypes within species should be especially prone to experience developmental system drift.
source: Ontogenetic stages that have an especially high incidence of mutationally-robust phenotypes within species should thus be especially prone to experience developmental system drift.
evidence: This is a prediction about the relationship between robustness and DSD across ontogeny.

claim: Degeneracy via partially redundant genetic network pathways provides another way that phenotypes could be robust to genetic perturbation, potentially allowing DSD to accumulate without yielding DMIs in F1 hybrids.
source: Degeneracy via partially redundant genetic network pathways provides another way that phenotypes could be robust to genetic perturbation, potentially allowing DSD to accumulate without yielding DMIs in F1 hybrids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how redundancy affects the relationship between DSD and DMIs.

claim: Genes associated with redundant networks evolve more quickly.
source: Indeed, genes associated with redundant networks evolve more quickly (Wagner, 2000; Kitami and Nadeau, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Translational buffering of gene expression leads to the inference that protein production shows much less misexpression than do mRNA transcripts in F1 hybrids.
source: Moreover, translational buffering of gene expression leads to the inference that protein production shows much less misexpression than do mRNA transcripts in F1 hybrids (Leducq et al., 2012; Khan et al., 2013; Artieri and Fraser, 2014; McManus et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Genetic networks important for development may be less disrupted in hybrids than transcriptome analyses might otherwise suggest.
source: And, it is fitness as a phenotype that is the ultimate readout of robustness. Consequently, genetic networks important for development may be less disrupted in hybrids than transcriptome analyses might otherwise suggest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the buffering of gene expression.

claim: Traits and sequences with greater propensity to diverge are said to be more evolvable.
source: Traits and sequences with greater propensity to diverge are said to be more evolvable (Wagner and Zhang, 2011).
evidence: This is a definition of evolvability supported by citation.

claim: Positive selection and multi-locus antagonistic coevolution will drive molecular evolution that is much more rapid than will genetic drift.
source: Moreover, positive selection and multi-locus antagonistic coevolution will drive molecular evolution that is much more rapid than will genetic drift.
evidence: This is a principle from evolutionary theory about rates of evolution under different selective regimes.

claim: Repeated adaptive evolution of orthologous genes in disparate lineages is implicated as a general feature of some types of phenotypic change, including aggregate effects of multiple mutations affecting the same locus.
source: Repeated adaptive evolution of orthologous genes in disparate lineages is implicated as a general feature of some types of phenotypic change, including aggregate effects of multiple mutations affecting the same locus (Stern and Orgogozo, 2008; Martin and Orgogozo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The genes contributing to adaptive divergence may be especially likely to contribute to post-zygotic DMIs.
source: The genes contributing to such adaptive divergence may thus be especially likely to contribute to post-zygotic DMIs (Presgraves, 2010b), in addition to pre-mating, gametic, or ecological reproductive isolation barriers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Haldane's rule states that the heterogametic sex is more likely to suffer inviability or sterility in inter-species hybrids.
source: One developmentally predictable rule in evolution says something about sex: Haldane's rule, in which the heterogametic sex is more likely to suffer inviability or sterility in inter-species hybrids (Haldane, 1922; Delph and Demuth, 2016).
evidence: This is a well-established empirical pattern in speciation genetics supported by citations.

claim: Dominance theory provides one explanation for Haldane's rule: incompatibility loci linked to sex chromosomes will reveal themselves in F1 hybrids disproportionately for the sex that has only one copy of a given sex chromosome.
source: Dominance theory provides one explanation for this pattern: incompatibility loci linked to sex chromosomes will reveal themselves in F1 hybrids disproportionately for the sex that has only one copy of a given sex chromosome (Turelli and Orr, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: X-linked genes may show distinct patterns of misexpression in hybrids.
source: Consequently, X-linked genes may show distinct patterns of misexpression in hybrids (Moehring et al., 2007; Turner et al., 2014; Civetta, 2016; Sanchez-Ramirez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Developmental pathways related to spermatogenesis seem especially sensitive to disruption in hybrids, perhaps being predisposed to disproportionate compensatory cis-trans regulatory coevolution.
source: Developmental pathways related to spermatogenesis seem especially sensitive to disruption in hybrids, perhaps being predisposed to disproportionate compensatory cis-trans regulatory coevolution (Mack et al., 2016; Mack and Nachman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The rate of evolution for a coding sequence and its cis-regulatory regions correlate only weakly.
source: The rate of evolution for a coding sequence and its cis-regulatory regions, however, correlate only weakly (Castillo-Davis, 2004; Liao and Zhang, 2006; Tirosh and Barkai, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The strength and mode of selection affecting mutations to protein structure tells us little about the strength and mode of selection on mutations affecting expression, and vice versa.
source: This observation implies that the strength and mode of selection affecting mutations to protein structure tells us little about the strength and mode of selection on mutations affecting expression, and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference from the weak correlation between coding and regulatory evolution.

claim: Genes showing evidence of trans-regulatory divergence appear to evolve slower in their coding sequences than do genes with cis-regulatory divergence.
source: For example, genes showing evidence of trans-regulatory divergence appear to evolve slower in their coding sequences than do genes with cis-regulatory divergence (Goncalves et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical work.

claim: DMIs due to misregulation generally involve non-compensatory evolution of both cis- and trans-regulators of expression.
source: And, DMIs due to misregulation generally involve non-compensatory evolution of both cis- and trans-regulators of expression (Ortíz-Barrientos et al., 2006; Mack and Nachman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Regulatory divergence involving reinforcing cis+trans changes (thought to result from directional selection within species) may actually be less likely to create DMIs than changes with opposing cis-trans effects (thought to result from stabilizing selection within species).
source: Specifically, regulatory divergence involving reinforcing cis+trans changes (thought to result from directional selection within species) may actually be less likely to create DMIs than changes with opposing cis-trans effects (thought to result from stabilizing selection within species) (Mack et al., 2016) (but see Tulchinsky et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical and theoretical work, with a caveat.

claim: Transcription factors experience faster sequence evolution than other genes in the genome.
source: From the perspective of gene regulatory networks, transcription factors experience faster sequence evolution than other genes in the genome (Gilad et al., 2006; Haerty et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: piRNA genes turnover rapidly and are implicated in hybrid dysfunction.
source: piRNA genes also turnover rapidly and are implicated in hybrid dysfunction (Assis and Kondrashov, 2009; Bagijn et al., 2012; Kelleher et al., 2012), along with other classes of regulatory endogenous small RNAs (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Reproductive isolation between species need not only involve classic regulators of development, as attested by incompatibilities that commonly seem to involve chromosome segregation and cyto-nuclear interactions.
source: Reproductive isolation between species need not only involve classic regulators of development, however, as attested by incompatibilities that commonly seem to involve chromosome segregation and cyto-nuclear interactions (Blackman, 2016; Lima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Mitochondrial genes experience adaptive molecular evolution.
source: Despite the fundamental role of the mitochondrial genome in energy metabolism, mitochondrial genes experience adaptive molecular evolution (Bazin et al., 2006) and mito-nuclear incompatibilities can provide important reproductive barriers between species (Hill, 2015; Lima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Mito-nuclear incompatibilities can provide important reproductive barriers between species.
source: Despite the fundamental role of the mitochondrial genome in energy metabolism, mitochondrial genes experience adaptive molecular evolution (Bazin et al., 2006) and mito-nuclear incompatibilities can provide important reproductive barriers between species (Hill, 2015; Lima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Gene duplication is a powerful factor in the evolution of phenotypic novelty.
source: Gene duplication is a powerful factor in the evolution of phenotypic novelty (Kaessmann, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Regulatory or structural subfunctionalization in the evolution of gene copies following duplication could lead to dysfunction in hybrids and so contribute to a DMI.
source: Moreover, regulatory or structural subfunctionalization in the evolution of gene copies following duplication could lead to dysfunction in hybrids and so contribute to a DMI (Mack and Nachman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: A DMI could result from 'divergent resolution' in the loss of alternate copies in different species for functionally equivalent gene duplicates.
source: Similarly, a DMI could result from 'divergent resolution' in the loss of alternate copies in different species for functionally equivalent gene duplicates (Lynch and Force, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The de novo origin of new genes can instigate species differences in gene network structure.
source: The de novo origin of new genes also can instigate species differences in gene network structure (Neme and Tautz, 2014), as could divergent use of alternative splice forms of a gene (Ortíz-Barrientos et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Gene expression profiles and genetic network architecture are dynamic over the course of ontogeny.
source: Gene expression profiles and genetic network architecture are dynamic over the course of ontogeny.
evidence: This is a general principle about development.

claim: Molecular evolution could differ for the distinct subsets of genes associated with different stages of development.
source: This dynamism suggests that molecular evolution could differ for the distinct subsets of genes associated with different stages of development (Box 3).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the dynamism of gene expression.

claim: Stages especially prone to rapid molecular evolution, of coding sequences or regulatory elements, may also translate into a greater incidence of DMIs.
source: Stages especially prone to rapid molecular evolution, of coding sequences or regulatory elements, may also translate into a greater incidence of DMIs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the relationship between molecular evolution and DMI incidence.

claim: 147 studies involving 106 species quantified transcriptome, proteome, or related molecular data across multiple developmental stages.
source: In our search of the literature, we identified 147 studies involving 106 species that quantified transcriptome, proteome, or related molecular data across multiple developmental stages (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a summary of a literature search conducted by the authors.

claim: 40% of studies focus on embryogenesis only.
source: We found 40% of studies to focus on embryogenesis only.
evidence: This is a result from the authors' literature search.

claim: Over 60% of the studies included a comparative analysis of expression divergence between species (52%) or of DNA sequence divergence (13%).
source: Over 60% of the studies included a comparative analysis of expression divergence between species (52%) or of DNA sequence divergence (13%).
evidence: This is a result from the authors' literature search.

claim: The early conservation model derives from the fact that time is unidirectional, so changes early in development may cascade catastrophically as cell division and differentiation proceeds.
source: The early conservation model ('von Baer's third law') derives from the fact that time is unidirectional, so changes early in development may cascade catastrophically as cell division and differentiation proceeds.
evidence: This is an explanation of the logic behind the early conservation model.

claim: According to the early conservation model, genes expressed early in development would experience stronger purifying selection, with slower molecular and phenotypic evolution early in ontogeny.
source: Consequently, genes expressed early in development would experience stronger purifying selection, with slower molecular and phenotypic evolution early in ontogeny (Kalinka and Tomancak, 2012).
evidence: This is a prediction of the early conservation model supported by citation.

claim: The early conservation model is mostly applied to embryogenesis, with some empirical support from vertebrates based on gene expression divergence.
source: The early conservation model is mostly applied to embryogenesis, with some empirical support from vertebrates based on gene expression divergence (Roux and Robinson-Rechavi, 2008; Irie and Kuratani, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: If the likelihood of DMIs scales with rate of evolution, then we ought to expect post-zygotic reproductive isolation to be more likely to manifest later in development and that species at earlier stages of divergence would manifest defects later in development.
source: If the likelihood of DMIs scales with rate of evolution, then we ought to expect post-zygotic reproductive isolation to be more likely to manifest later in development and that species at earlier stages of divergence would manifest defects later in development.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the early conservation model.

claim: Early-acting incompatibilities may preclude detection of DMIs that would otherwise be revealed later.
source: A caveat about inferring the developmental timing of hybrid dysfunction is that early-acting incompatibilities may preclude detection of DMIs that would otherwise be revealed later (see uniform chance model, below).
evidence: This is a logical caveat about interpreting patterns of hybrid dysfunction.

claim: The 'uniform chance' model represents a null model for the manifestation of hybrid incompatibilities over the course of ontogeny.
source: We suggest that the 'uniform chance' model represents a null model for the manifestation of hybrid incompatibilities over the course of ontogeny.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework proposed by the authors.

claim: If molecular evolution is unbiased with respect to the timing of expression of genes that have diverged between species, then every point in development can be considered to have an equal chance of expressing a DMI to yield hybrid disruption of a tissue type or termination of development.
source: If molecular evolution is unbiased with respect to the timing of expression of genes that have diverged between species, then every point in development can be considered to have an equal chance of expressing a DMI to yield hybrid disruption of a tissue type or termination of development (Figure 1).
evidence: This is the logic of the uniform chance null model.

claim: The uniform chance model predicts a negative relationship of the genetic distance between species and the terminal stage to which hybrids develop.
source: This null model therefore predicts a negative relationship of the genetic distance between species and the terminal stage to which hybrids develop, and predicts that later stages will have more tissue types exhibiting dysfunction in hybrids.
evidence: This is a prediction of the uniform chance model.

claim: The mutation accumulation model of aging predicts that genes and genetic networks expressed earlier in development will evolve more slowly.
source: The mutation accumulation model of aging and senescence predicts that genes and genetic networks expressed earlier in development will evolve more slowly (Promislow and Tatar, 1998; Partridge, 2001).
evidence: This is a prediction of the mutation accumulation model supported by citations.

claim: The reproductive value of individuals declines following the onset of reproductive maturity, meaning that purifying selection is weaker against deleterious mutations that affect adult phenotypes relative to embryonic and juvenile phenotypes.
source: Here, the logic and developmental timing, however, is different from the early conservation model: the reproductive value of individuals declines following the onset of reproductive maturity, meaning that purifying selection is weaker against deleterious mutations that affect adult phenotypes relative to embryonic and juvenile phenotypes (Medawar, 1952; Flatt and Schmidt, 2009).
evidence: This is the logic of the mutation accumulation model supported by citations.

claim: The antagonistic pleiotropy model states that gain in fitness from traits that increase survival or reproduction early in life will experience disproportionate selection pressure.
source: Gain in fitness from traits that increase survival or reproduction early in life will experience disproportionate selection pressure.
evidence: This is a statement of the antagonistic pleiotropy model.

claim: According to the antagonistic pleiotropy model, positive selection may more fiercely favor beneficial mutations to genes expressed early in life, irrespective of negative pleiotropic consequences on fitness-related traits expressed later on.
source: Consequently, positive selection may more fiercely favor beneficial mutations to genes expressed early in life, irrespective of negative pleiotropic consequences on fitness-related traits expressed later on. This idea is the essence of the antagonistic pleiotropy model for the evolution of aging and senescence (Williams, 1957; Partridge, 2001; Flatt and Schmidt, 2009).
evidence: This is an explanation of the antagonistic pleiotropy model supported by citations.

claim: The antagonistic pleiotropy model ought to yield a signature of excess positive selection on genes first expressed at pre-reproductive stages.
source: In terms of molecular evolution, it ought to yield a signature of excess positive selection on genes first expressed at pre-reproductive stages (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a prediction of the antagonistic pleiotropy model.

claim: The hourglass model is a pattern in search of a mechanism that derives from classic phenotypic observations of a 'phylotypic stage' in mid-embryogenesis, a point of greatest morphological similarity across organisms.
source: The hourglass model is a pattern in search of a mechanism that derives from classic phenotypic observations of a 'phylotypic stage' in mid-embryogenesis, a point of greatest morphological similarity across organisms.
evidence: This is a description of the hourglass model.

claim: Profiles of gene expression divergence between species are often interpreted to be consistent with the hourglass pattern.
source: Profiles of gene expression divergence between species, a molecular phenotype, also are often interpreted to be consistent with this pattern (Raff, 1996; Kalinka and Tomancak, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: It is proposed that the phylotypic stage may coincide with developmental periods of intense integration of distinct cell lineages, often around gastrulation.
source: Ontogenetic trends in genetic network architecture may provide some intuition, as it is proposed that the phylotypic stage may coincide with developmental periods of intense integration of distinct cell lineages, often around gastrulation (Levin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Theory predicts more rapid accumulation of mutations to genes acting in the earliest genetic networks that derive from maternal resources, leading to their unusually fast molecular evolution with the potential to drive DSD and DMIs.
source: For example, theory predicts more rapid accumulation of mutations to genes acting in the earliest genetic networks that derive from maternal resources, leading to their unusually fast molecular evolution with the potential to drive DSD and DMIs (Demuth and Wade, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Faster-than-anticipated molecular evolution at the very earliest stages of development might also arise from especially high robustness of genetic networks involving maternally deposited gene products, or from co-evolutionary dynamics associated with parent-offspring or other genomic conflicts.
source: Faster-than-anticipated molecular evolution at the very earliest stages of development might also arise from especially high robustness of genetic networks involving maternally deposited gene products, or from co-evolutionary dynamics associated with parent-offspring or other genomic conflicts (Brandvain and Haig, 2005; Crespi and Nosil, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Sexual selection and sexual conflict that occurs within and between the sexes for reproductive adults can promote rapid phenotypic and molecular evolution via positive selection, especially in reproduction- and gamete-related traits.
source: Sexual selection and sexual conflict that occurs within and between the sexes for reproductive adults can promote rapid phenotypic and molecular evolution via positive selection, especially in reproduction- and gamete-related traits (Swanson and Vacquier, 2002; Mank, 2017; Rowe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Genes controlling gamete traits may be especially prone to rapid molecular evolution.
source: Genes controlling gamete traits may be especially prone to rapid molecular evolution (Swanson and Vacquier, 2002), with the effects on hybrids potentially reflected in the earliest-stage zygotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Speciation genetics research has incorporated the idea of rapid evolution of sex-limited genes into the 'faster male' theory for Haldane's rule and into the explanation for why hybrid sterility often appears to arise earlier in the speciation process than does hybrid inviability.
source: Speciation genetics research has incorporated this idea of rapid evolution of sex-limited genes into the 'faster male' theory for Haldane's rule and into the explanation for why hybrid sterility often appears to arise earlier in the speciation process than does hybrid inviability (Coyne, 1989; Wu and Davis, 1993; Ortíz-Barrientos et al., 2006; Presgraves, 2010a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Genes with sex-limited expression may experience weaker purifying selection, meaning greater accumulation of divergence between species.
source: In addition to the possibility of more prevalent positive selection on genes with sex-limited expression, they may also experience weaker purifying selection (Dapper and Wade, 2016). Weaker purifying selection means greater accumulation of divergence between species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Weaker efficacy of selection on sex-limited genes arises because half of the individuals in the population, one sex or the other, do not express the gene and so mask the effects of new detrimental mutations.
source: This weaker efficacy of selection arises because half of the individuals in the population, one sex or the other, do not express the gene and so mask the effects of new detrimental mutations.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism for weaker selection on sex-limited genes.

claim: Rapid evolution of maternal-provisioning genes may lead to incompatibilities when they interact with zygotically-expressed genes in inter-species hybrids, potentially elevating the incidence of mid-embryonic hybrid dysfunction independently of any temporal changes in genetic network modularity or robustness.
source: Rapid evolution of maternal-provisioning genes may lead to incompatibilities when they interact with zygotically-expressed genes in inter-species hybrids, potentially elevating the incidence of mid-embryonic hybrid dysfunction independently of any temporal changes in genetic network modularity or robustness.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the consequences of rapid evolution of maternal genes.

claim: Genetic incompatibilities involving uniparentally inherited genetic factors may lead to predictable asymmetries in reproductive isolation between species pairs.
source: Genetic incompatibilities involving uniparentally inherited genetic factors also may lead to predictable asymmetries in reproductive isolation between species pairs (Turelli and Moyle, 2007), including roles for genes encoded on sex chromosomes and mitochondrial genomes (Bolnick et al., 2008; Barreto et al., 2018; Cutter, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: C. elegans embryonic cell numbers grow approximately exponentially until ~520 cells upon which cell count increases relatively slowly to the 959 somatic and ~2000 germline cells that comprise the adult hermaphrodite animal.
source: Taking C. elegans development as a point of reference, embryonic cell numbers grow approximately exponentially until ~520 cells upon which cell count increases relatively slowly to the 959 somatic and ~2000 germline cells that comprise the adult hermaphrodite animal (Giurumescu et al., 2012; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Cell lineages derived from five blastomeres in C. elegans exhibit distinct transcriptome profiles in ontogenetic timecourses.
source: Cell lineages derived from five blastomeres exhibit distinct transcriptome profiles in ontogenetic timecourses (Hashimshony et al., 2015), with single-cell transcriptome sequencing of embryos in a time series showing even finer resolution (Packer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The number of genes expressed in C. elegans increases over most of embryogenesis, with relatively similar numbers of genes expressed at stages post-hatching.
source: The number of genes expressed increases over most of embryogenesis, with relatively similar numbers of genes expressed at stages post-hatching (Boeck et al., 2016; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The change in identity of expressed genes in C. elegans is greatest early in embryogenesis (primarily due to down-regulation) and late in embryogenesis (primarily due to up-regulation).
source: The change in identity of expressed genes, however, is greatest early in embryogenesis (primarily due to down-regulation) and late in embryogenesis (primarily due to up-regulation) (Boeck et al., 2016; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Gene connectivity in C. elegans peaks in early embryogenesis, declining until a spike in adulthood.
source: Gene connectivity peaks in early embryogenesis, declining until a spike in adulthood (Liu and Robinson-Rechavi, 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Cellular development in Caenorhabditis embryos is conserved across species, being nearly indistinguishable at least to the 350-cell stage.
source: Cellular development in embryos is conserved across species, being nearly indistinguishable at least to the 350-cell stage (Zhao et al., 2008; Memar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In hybrid crosses of most Caenorhabditis species pairs, embryos arrest around gastrulation.
source: In hybrid crosses of most species pairs, however, embryos arrest around gastrulation (Baird and Yen, 2000; Baird and Seibert, 2013), near the time that expression divergence appears minimized across Caenorhabditis (Levin et al., 2012) and that expression-weighted coding sequence divergence is lowest (Cutter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Coding sequences with fastest molecular evolution in Caenorhabditis show peak expression very early in embryogenesis or toward adulthood.
source: Coding sequences with fastest molecular evolution show peak expression very early in embryogenesis or toward adulthood (Cutter and Ward, 2005; Cutter et al., 2019; Box 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Hybrids of C. briggsae and C. nigoni show high embryonic inviability, but those genetically identical individuals that hatch successfully exhibit little larval mortality.
source: Hybrids of C. briggsae and C. nigoni show high embryonic inviability, but those genetically identical individuals that hatch successfully exhibit little larval mortality (Bundus et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Gene misexpression is widespread in adults of both sexes for C. briggsae and C. nigoni hybrids.
source: Gene misexpression is widespread in adults of both sexes for these hybrids (Sanchez-Ramirez et al., 2020) and misregulation of small-RNAs in hybrid genetic backgrounds is implicated in spermatogenic dysfunction (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Coding sequences expressed across D. melanogaster development show slowest evolution in mid- to late-embryogenesis.
source: Coding sequences expressed across D. melanogaster development show slowest evolution in mid- to late-embryogenesis (Davis et al., 2005; Coronado-Zamora et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The faster sequence evolution of maternally deposited transcripts in early Drosophila embryogenesis is due disproportionately to non-adaptive divergence whereas it is adaptive divergence that is disproportionately implicated in faster sequence evolution of genes expressed post-embryonically.
source: The faster sequence evolution of maternally deposited transcripts in early embryogenesis is due disproportionately to non-adaptive divergence whereas it is adaptive divergence that is disproportionately implicated in faster sequence evolution of genes expressed post-embryonically (Coronado-Zamora et al., 2019; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Gene connectivity in Drosophila shows a peak in early embryogenesis and in adulthood.
source: Gene connectivity similarly shows a peak in early embryogenesis and in adulthood (Liu and Robinson-Rechavi, 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Transcriptome divergence across Drosophila species is low throughout most of embryogenesis and highest after reproductive maturity; within embryogenesis, however, expression divergence is greatest at the earliest stages.
source: Transcriptome divergence across species, however, is low throughout most of embryogenesis and highest after reproductive maturity; within embryogenesis, however, expression divergence is greatest at the earliest stages (Kalinka et al., 2010; Liu and Robinson-Rechavi, 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Sterility tends to arise before inviability in hybrids of a given phylogenetic distance in Drosophila.
source: Sterility tends to arise before inviability in hybrids of a given phylogenetic distance in Drosophila (Coyne and Orr, 1997), and hybrid misexpression among spermatogenesis genes is much more pronounced in adults than in late-stage larvae (Moehring et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Genes with greater tissue-specificity in Drosophila show faster coding sequence evolution.
source: Genes with greater tissue-specificity show faster coding sequence evolution (Larracuente et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Hybrid misexpression in Drosophila less often involves genes implicated in transcriptional regulation than expected.
source: Hybrid misexpression less often involves genes implicated in transcriptional regulation than expected (Moehring et al., 2007), and defects of chromosome condensation in mitosis, nucleoporins, and transcriptional regulators of selfish elements have been implicated in the inviability of hybrid larvae (Orr et al., 1997; Barbash et al., 2003; Tang and Presgraves, 2009; Satyaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Defects of chromosome condensation in mitosis, nucleoporins, and transcriptional regulators of selfish elements have been implicated in the inviability of Drosophila hybrid larvae.
source: Hybrid misexpression less often involves genes implicated in transcriptional regulation than expected (Moehring et al., 2007), and defects of chromosome condensation in mitosis, nucleoporins, and transcriptional regulators of selfish elements have been implicated in the inviability of hybrid larvae (Orr et al., 1997; Barbash et al., 2003; Tang and Presgraves, 2009; Satyaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The developmental timing of hybrid inviability in frogs and toads enjoys much richer literature than for many other systems.
source: The developmental timing of hybrid inviability in frogs and toads enjoys much richer literature than for many other systems.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The developmental stages of hybrid inviability are described for over 600 inter-species Bufo cross combinations, with late-stage hybrid dysfunction being most prevalent for species pairs that are less genetically divergent.
source: The developmental stages of hybrid inviability are described for over 600 inter-species Bufo cross combinations, with late-stage hybrid dysfunction being most prevalent for species pairs that are less genetically divergent (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2 which shows data from the literature.

claim: Comparative transcriptome analysis across Xenopus laevis and X. tropicalis embryonic development showed changes in expression profiles of many genes despite a background of conservation in expression for most genes.
source: One key exception among anurans is for the model species Xenopus laevis and X. tropicalis: comparative transcriptome analysis across their embryonic development showed changes in expression profiles of many genes despite a background of conservation in expression for most genes (Yanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Earlier stages of Xenopus embryogenesis showed greater divergence in gene expression.
source: Interestingly, earlier stages of embryogenesis showed greater divergence in gene expression (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2.
